turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: So do you feel like you’ve had a chance to put your theory into practice then?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yeah, definitely and seeing like, I’ve learnt about management systems and got used to a system here, so actually seeing it working in real life and finding the pitfalls and finding what works and what doesn’t work and seeing how different the reactions are as well.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Ok, do you think that apart from technical skills, skills from uni like communication and organisational skills, have they been useful too?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yes. Huhum. Communication especially. I have learnt a lot more communication on the site being here, especially using things like Outlook which I never really use at Uni. So there are lot of skills that I’ve had to develop and learn. and I’ve had a lot of training in the company on that and on-going training.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: What sort of training have you been doing?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Um, I’ve had, I never knew how to, um I’ve had to take on, we have a little intranet system and so our department has intranet pages and so, that’s one of my responsibilities is to look after that and build it and put information on it. And when they first told me I was sort of ‘Oh my goodness!’ I can’t do that, so like they trained me from scratch and that’s really good. Documentations, we have a big documentation system which is quite complex so like training on that and Powerpoint and one of the… Also presentation skills as well. I did a four day course on presentation skills and how to group’s attention and putting things across.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Is there anything that you wish you had learnt before you started the placement?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: I think Outlook would be a, like learning to use Outlook in an efficient manner beforehand is a key one I think. I think every company uses Outlook (laughs) and its sort of, it’s essential really.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: At [University] they don’t seem to be very hot on using the email system, do they?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: No. It’s not so easy to use, you’re not integrated into the system very quickly. You’re just told right there’s your computer. There’s your login, how to login, and that’s about it. You’re not really told what packages there are and what you can use.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK, were you taught anything about health and safety at uni?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yeah, we’ve done quite a lot on health and safety because it was an integrated part of my degree in some senses because all, everyone else on my scheme are doing health and safety, pretty much. So I was sort of thrown in with them, so I’ve done a lot of health and safety yeah.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Has that been useful or have you had to do more site specific health and safety here?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Um, like everyone goes through an induction where they go through site specific and general health and safety practices. But because I work in health and safety, environmental health and safety, I don’t really use my health and safety knowledge that much at all really, because I’ve got the health and safety team there, and they’re specifically knowledge, it’s not as if I was in a department where there might be a need to have a person EHS wise, altogether rather than health and safety separately and environmental separately, so, I don’t use it that much to be honest.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Ok do you think that there is anything else the university could have done to prepare you for coming on placement?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Um, I don’t know, cos’ I mean, until you actually get to a place and see what you’re doing and actually get in there and do it, you don’t really and I can imagine different places have very different ways, so I can’t see how the Uni could actually prepare you - it would be a nightmare. You would have to say every individually done and they are not going to know what the companies like really unless they have had other students go.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Ok, how did you find the transition from education to work?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Um, the early mornings were an interesting one. (Laughs).

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: What time do you start work at?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: We have flexi-time, we’re supposed to be on anytime from 10 o’clock, you got to do 10-3 which are core hours, but otherwise it’s flexi-time, but because of what I have to do, I do a lot of monitoring out on the site and to get on permits I have to get out on site by about half eight, quarter past eight, so I’m in to work about quarter to eight, so I’m up at half six every morning which is like a bit of a shock to the system. But then you get to finish early. It was sort of, we were eased into it quite gently, because we have a regular thing called Summer working hours where on a Friday you can finish at 12.00 if you do enough hours through the rest of the week. So you get the whole afternoon. So you’re eased into it gently. I think it wasn’t too bad, but it did take in some ways it did take a while getting used to, building up your stamina to be able to work a full day. And sort of keeping your attention span on it all day. For the first sort of two months, or three months really, it was absorb information, you’re being thrown information and trying to keep on top of it all, it’s a bit scary really.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Ok do you feel like have to face any new issues at all, like office politics?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yes (Laughing) Office politics is quite a big one.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Were you expecting that?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: I was in a sense because I’ve worked in big kitchens and lots of organisations and there’s always politics with everything and it’s trying to keep out of it and trying not to get involved, which is really hard work. Especially the longer you stay, the more you find yourself getting dragged into it. And you’re like trying to keep quiet when you know (laughs).

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: How do you feel about going back to uni when you’ve finished?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: I think it’s going to be hard. It’s going to be - because motivation for work is completely different, to being at Uni, cos’ Uni you just plod along, everyone’s laid back and it’s ‘oh yeah it’ll be done’ whereas at work you’ve got to do this and you’ve got to have it done by this time. So it’s sort of that and I think, in some ways I think the amount of work will decrease and I’ll be like, ‘ok, I’m bored now’. I want to carry on doing something real, so I think that’s going to be quite a hard one to get back into the swing of it, I think I’ll have it sorted by about half way through (laughs).

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Do you think there are any other differences between work and uni?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Um, Uni is a lot more laid back, and the way people talk to each other a lot. Sort of sitting in meetings sometimes, hearing the different way people talk and try and get their point across is quite an interesting one, rather than at Uni you just like fight for your corner a bit and it’s all sort politically done, like oh no, I can’t say that, so it’s quite interesting in that way.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Do you think that work and uni have different goals and priorities?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Definitely. It always ends up being back to money situation at work, rather than at uni. I think it’s sort of the nature of a lot of the things you do at Uni is completely different, it’s all theoretical, it’s very rarely application, so its going to be a lot harder to get, compare them in some ways.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Do you think there is scope for more practical work on your course?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: I think it is quite, already there are some, we do get fed some good projects which are work connected, so we do get out into the workplace. But at the end of the day we just produce reports and then it’s up to the company whether they want to actually put them in. So they could be completely off track, but it’s still a report and you still get marks for it. So I think rather than, it’s coming back to work its getting that sort of its all connected to work, can we afford it, is it feasible in that way, and its also the other thing that its different is because everything takes four times as long here at work than in does at uni.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Is that when you hit problems and stuff like that?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yes it goes through nine million other people before it comes back and it still hasn’t been resolved until it gets sent all the way round the people again (laughing).

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Can you tell me what your team do and what your role involves?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Um, it’s, our team is the environmental department for the whole of manufacturing on site. So we look after and make sure that we don’t put anything in the wrong places. We deal with all our waste in an appropriate manner. We’ve got [name], which is our environmental management system and so we look after that and we keep on track of that, and deal with and co-ordinate any actions that we may have from any audits. We go out and actually audit the departments, make sure they’re doing everything correctly. We just keep everyone in tow, make sure they’re doing the right thing. And we have a number of databases which we keep up to date, which the site all put into, so we’re keeping that up to date and working quite well. Um, my job is specifically, I do a bit of everything, it’s quite good. One of my main jobs is to do with atmospheric monitoring so we go round and actually physically go and set up monitoring on various stacks to make sure we’re within the compliance.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Do you have to report those to Government?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yeah we report that to the Environment Agency and to corporate which is in New York, so they know what we’re doing and the environment agency knows what we’re doing, and it’s quite interesting because corporate will be stronger, more heavy handed than the environment agency.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Is that just a company thing or are they harder on stuff like that in America?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yes. They’re actually softer in America so it’s quite interesting working for an American company because the American issues, they don’t believe in certain things which we believe in so it’s like we’re fighting a battle, it’s like hitting your head against a brick wall sometimes because you’re like this is really happening. Things like global warming, they don’t believe in global warming. They don’t recognise it. But what happens is that because it’s such a big company everyone’s fighting for - although it’s a big company and it’s one company, different sites around the world are fighting for the work, so if we have good results, then we’ll get the work. So that’s why, the reason why it’s sort of like that

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Was that surprising to you?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: It was in some ways, yeah. It get’s very complicated because there’s. It’s basically split up into three mini companies almost. You’ve got manufacturing, we’ve got global operations, so the people that coordinate everything around the world, and we’ve got research and development. So there’s the three companies, they’re all sort of nudging around each other and who gets ranked where. It’s quite interesting sometimes.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Do [company] employ a lot of women?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yeah, I mean we’ve got in my team at the moment, there’s 6 of us, yeah, 6 of us, and well 6 in total in the team and 4 of us are women and then like in health and safety there is 7 and they have got 3 so there are, it is quite evenly distributed and the majority of the departments have got almost half and half. It’s like some of the operators they don’t tend to be women because of the nature of what they are dealing with, and women just don’t like, like. So you go into some areas and its very male dominated and they haven’t seen a woman for like 12 hours and you walk in with your paper and you get all kinds of comments.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: What like?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Well, sort of they’re always apologising for their language or they’re always, make a joke and then be ‘oh, sorry, women in the room’. Cos’ we have a lot of contractors in as well and with all contractors walking around and the scaffolders and the builders, sometimes some of the things they come out with it’s like, then they suddenly realize that you’re in the room and they’re like ‘ooh sorry’. It’s quite a nice gentle banter really that goes on. I think you have to be quite,you can’t be too sensitive about things. If you were too shy and sensitive, you’d be eaten up alive. You have to stand your ground.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: What sort of reactions do you give them then?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Well I give them as good as I get. So, its equal. And you have a laugh. If you give them respect, they’ll give you respect back, so.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: So are the jokes and that between you and the operators, rather than you and your colleagues?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yeah. It’s not between, yeah.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK, do [company] have a programme or structure in place for placement students to follow?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Erm, not really,

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Do they set any targets?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Because industrial trainees are put in so many different departments and their roles can vary so much over the period, over the site, HR don’t really put in any structure. Its up to our Line Manager to deal with and I have got a very good Line Manager so she treats me like one of the team and there is about four Performance Managers and they put down the objectives and responsibilities and how to improve things and what I need training on and things like that, so she just keeps. So, if she’s looking at one specific thing in a monthly meeting, then she’ll also look at say a similar thing with me and say well can we apply it to you? You’re only here for a year, but, like last month we went through what we wanted to do in the future what were the sort of future objectives and so we went through things like that and what were the options and jobs I could do and things like that.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Do you like having that in place?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yeah it gives it structure and it gives us a chance to sit down and actually go through what I’ve done during the month and what I’ve achieved and where if I’m struggling anywhere and at that point I can say ‘oh, help, I’m sinking here.’ Or I mean I can go to her any time during the month but specifically that meeting’s there for that purpose and then she can give me more work or less work or reorganise myself.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Yes, ok, so is your job what you thought it would be doing when you applied for it?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: I didn’t really know what I was meant to be doing. The advert was vague to say the least - it was a gobbledegook thing saying that you’re going to working in the environmental department but didn’t really say what it was or what I was going to be doing. So it was sort of, my first day I was like what am I actually doing (laughs). But it’s quite good because the way our department is set up people have got their specialities, so I’m getting to work with each individual member of the team. So like [name] who you met she deals with environmental monitoring and our environmental management systems. So I work quite a lot with her and then we’ve got another guy who’s specialised in all the legalities of everything, legislation and things like that so I work with him a bit.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: So you’re getting a taste of everything?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yeah. I’ve been doing work for another guy who deals with all of our waste streams, so it’s quite interesting I get a full range of, it doesn’t get boring.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Do you feel like you’ve been given an appropriate level of responsibility?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Mmm, I mean my jobs, they’ve been doing quite industrial placements in my department for I think it’s 7,8,9 years, so it’s quite a long time. Each year it changes slightly and you start off with very little responsibility and then it grows and grows and grows depending on what you feel like, depending on what’s going on. So I mean the first, up till Christmas I was doing, I always had someone with me when I was out on the site and then after Christmas it was, it got to the point where I was doing monitoring on my own, well for the easier things and where I got to know what I was doing, so I had those sort of responsibilities. And like the sites’ Jamboree, which we have just done now, that was solely my responsibility to, I was just put into a team of three and all of us IT’s [industrial trainees], we were just told to do a stand for the Jamboree. So my responsibilities are growing all the time and different things like that. And I have got a job on at the moment looking at (inaudible) depleting compound chemicals around the site and that information that I am gathering will report directly to senior level management, so things like that, my core responsibilities are growing and I think it does develop with the time and if I feel that I am being sort of buried or feel it’s too much, they, [name] will take it off at any time.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: So your supervisor is approachable enough for you to go and say ‘help’?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yeah or when she sees me going ‘I’m drowning, pick me up please’, so that’s quite good, um.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: So do you feel you were given more responsibility at the right time or would you have like it earlier?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Um, I think it’s been sort of drip fed slowly so I haven’t really noticed it, so I think it’s been done in a very good manner, in terms of it’s just gone on so steadily that you don’t really notice it.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: How would you summarise your placement experience so far then?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: It’s been good; it’s been good fun. Um, because there are, I think there’s about 25 industrial trainees on manufacturing, and there are a lot more on research, but… So it’s almost, we’ve got a little group of us who get on really well and we all live in five minutes radius. So it’s like being at uni in some ways because you’ve got that sort of young structure around you, and we obviously socialise together so you’ve got that and then you’ve got work and there’s always that point of contact if you feel like you need to talk to someone you’ve always got some other people in a similar situation who you can - and sort of like my team are like quite a close team and then brought, let me come in quite a bit, really well, so I don’t really think of myself as like a one year outsider, ‘oh I’m just here for a year, that’s it’.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: You feel like you have been treated as a permanent member of staff?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yes definitely.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: You mentioned having other placement students here, do you think that there are any disadvantages to that?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: I don’t think so, I think it’s an advantage if anything because you end up getting more contacts round the site so people come to me for information and odd bits of things to know what’s going on on site because I’ve got a full feel, so I’ve got that sort of structure or network on a very low level and we’ve all got completely random bits of information which they’d never find out so there is a good structure there. And that also helps you to get to know everyone else on site. You don’t obviously know the full 900 but you get to know quite a lot, you get to know faces and you think ah yes he works in so and so. It works quite well that way, and it also gives you the confidence because you’ve got that to fall back on as a sort of safety net.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: What would say have been the best and the worst things about the placement so far?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Erm, best things, working in such a close knit team and working on, getting the chance to work on everything and anything I want to. If I want to work on a specific area I can just say I want to work on it and I’ll get moved to it. Erm, and working for such a large company is a good sort of base, I think it’s a good standing really.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: You’ve got the benefits of a big company, but at the same time you’re in a small team?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yeah, so it’s got the right proportion in some ways. And working with so many different people as well. Erm, disadvantages. Erm, I don’t know. It’s, I think it’ll make it harder to go back to uni, definitely. To go back into study mode, to go back into academic, because you get used to sort of working and talking and doing things in a work mode, rather than in academic. Erm, I don’t know.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Would you recommend other people to do a placement?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Definitely.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: And would you recommend them to come here to do a placement?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yes. I mean it’s got … because they’ve got the experience of having trainees and students, they know the pitfalls, so they try and help you round. I mean, simple things like accommodation. They put us up for the first two weeks in erm digs. So we had a family who were already there and sort of in the area, who knew the area, didn’t necessarily work with the company, but were there. And it sort of gave you a base to start off with. So even if the other trainees weren’t around, you still had, it wasn’t as if you were on your own and sort of, lonely almost. You always had people around and people to talk to.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Did you have inductions or anything with the other placement students?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yes, they basically taken on all industrial trainees over, either they start at the start of one month, or the start of the second month. So, you’ve always got other trainees with you, as you start at the same time. Certainly you finish all at the same time, so it’s quite good. You’re straight away, you’re introduced to people, a similar age group, maybe not in the same department or anywhere, you might not work with them at all during the time, but you know they’re there.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: It’s quite good knowing that you’re not the only new person

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yes, so that’s quite good. And if you ever have any problems, there’s housing people on site that, and you’ve got HR that are you can always fall back on, so it’s got the structure and everything to help you as much as possible, so it’s not too daunting. Erm, I also think that you need the experience to get a job nowadays. You need to have at least a year’s experience and if people, if you just go through uni and through school, and don’t actually go and see the real world, you live on cloud cuckoo land half the time. Erm, and sort of getting that experience I think is a very good base. Especially for the future ‘cos you learn so much which you wouldn’t learn at uni, but you can just then take back to uni.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: So you think it will help you in your final year as well?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yes definitely.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Do you think that you’ve changed personally as a result of the placement?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: I think so. Erm, we were having this discussion the other night. We all feel so much older (laughing). We’re all like, we were sort of watching other students who, are just at college or uni, and we were like ‘no, we weren’t like that’.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: You’re like grown-ups now?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yeah. (laughing) It’s scary, we’re all grown up. It’s like you’ve lost that sort of kid inside or play attitude, it’s all so serious. (laughing)

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Do you think you are more confident or independent?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: I think so, yeah. I think is the confidence thing, that you can go and sort of greet different people you don’t know or who you know are managers, and talk to them as if they were on the same level. But it’s being able to talk senior managers but then down to the operators, sort of at the operators level. So its getting the way to talk to people in different ways, is a major thing I think, which you would never learn at uni.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Have you had to do a lot of team work here?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yes

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: You touched on this earlier, but how do you think that doing team work at uni compares to doing team work in the workplace?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Erm, there’s some similarities because your relying on people to pull their weight and some people don’t, and it’s the same at uni. Erm, but in other ways it’s different because there is more sort of mature, sort of look on it, ‘it’s got to be done’. And there’s pressures of other people to get the work done so, so there’s that sort of aspect. And I think the team’s are, people bring in so many different information from their different departments. A lot of the teams that I work on, will be people from all over the site, so you get a full sort of range of knowledge, and it gets quite interesting sometimes.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Because of that, do you think that you maybe have clearer roles within the team?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: In some ways, yes. But I think it depends on what the team are doing. I think it, sometimes everyone just muddles through, but then if it’s talking sort of within the department team, we all have our own roles. Erm and my role is always to back someone up, so I’ll be doing something. But if you’re talking site wise then it is sort of you’ve got your own roles and knowledge bases and it’ll always end up being connected to what you do, so yes I suppose in some ways it is clearer.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Do you think that makes it easier to do group work?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Sometimes not. Because there are some, it’s where you get some overlapping of departments and knowledge and who’s responsible for this, and who’s responsible for this and all that. So things get missed out, rather than if you have like a haphazard way you know that someone’s going to cover that or even if it gets covered twice, at least it gets covered. Rather than like sometimes people are like ‘well it’s that department, their department to do that’. So sometimes there’s big holes in things.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Do you think that doing team work at uni has helped you?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: I think so yeah. I think at uni it teaches you to sort of listen to everyone and try and get everyone, sort of, what they’re stronger at and what their weaker at and try and pull that information from everyone. And so yeah it does help quite a bit.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Ok. Have there been any particular people you’ve liked or disliked working with here?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yes (laughing). Erm, there was a member of my department, who’s luckily gone on maternity leave, erm that, she had a serious attitude problem and erm upset a lot of people, and she spoke down towards people, especially me because I was the low person, bottom of the pile. And erm, some of the things. I mean she erm. The one time, it was our Christmas dinner and like my senior senior manager was sitting right opposite us and she just started putting me down It just went straight over my head, ‘cos I’d sort of got used to it and I think everyone else round us was like ‘oh my goodness, how can you say that’. Erm, but across the sort of, you just get used to it and ignore it, and try not to work with her as much as possible, which is, it sounds bad, but everyone else does. But it was the whole team.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: So she was like it with everyone?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yeah, so it wasn’t just me specifically. So there are things like that. I think she’s like the person I wouldn’t work with, or try not to work, probably the only person really that I’ve had a problem with. But everyone else, I think is sort of I get on well with.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Have you been given a mentor at all?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: [Name] is sort of my mentor slash supervisor. Erm, but unofficially. Like we sit in a little cubby hole together, erm and so she sort of makes sure I’m ok and then we’ve always got [name] who’s my boss and line manager. But officially I haven’t been given a mentor. So, I have got a system in place, but unofficially.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Do you think it would have been a good idea to have an official mentor?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: I don’t think so, because I think it’s sort of, everyone takes, sort of everyone looks after me. It’s quite sweet really, ‘cos like everyone’s like, because [name] was off last week, so I had people just checking on me, saying ‘oh, are you alright, are you okay, are you still there?’ So everyone takes it on themselves to sort of make sure, and especially if I’m working with a specific person, then they’ll make sure I’m ok, so I’ve got support all round.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: How would you describe the role of a mentor then?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Erm, someone, if you’ve got a problem, to go and talk to. Erm, someone to make sure that you’re not drowning under the pressure or anything and if you’ve got a problem with someone on site or, you could just go and talk to them about it and see how you can actually resolve anything. Sort of a general problem solver.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Is there anyone that you would regard as a role model?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: I don’t know. I think everyone in my department really are all role models because they’re doing lots of interesting work which I would sort of be very interested in doing in the future. So sort of learning and they’re all very professional with the way they work. So sort (of picking up, them or a different team really?).

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Ok, has anyone from uni been to visit you yet? A placement tutor?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Erm, [name] who’s the scheme leader came to visit me and he, we sat down with both [name] and [name] and we went and told him what we were doing and they told him what they thought of me and things like that and sort of the relevance of the degree.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Do you think that was useful?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: I think it was nice to have that sort of all, all us all in uni at the back there and I think they, I think [placement tutor] found it very useful. Erm, sort of seeing what I do and the relevance of it all. So I think it was good for both sides. Erm, and it gave me a chance to talk about next year and dissertations and things like that.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Do you have to do any work for uni from the placement?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: No. I don’t have to do anything. I mean the thing was just for [name] to come down and make sure I’m okay. Erm, so I haven’t really got any proper work but I can sort of think about disseration and start doing work if I want to for my dissertation.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Do you think you’ll use anything from here for your dissertation?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: I might do, erm, but it’s a case of finding something that’s suitable and that’s, I’ve got time to fix it down and do work, take something from here. Erm, and it’s, at the moment, it’s not going to happen. I’ve got too much work on.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: So, if you had any problems here would you be happy to go and speak to [placement tutor]?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yeah, definitely. I’d just pick up the phone or email him. Erm, I know he’d be able to sort it because, he, especially now he’s been down and met my manager and met my supervisor.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: How far into the placement were you when he visited?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: He only came in January, so it’s sort of about half way through. Erm, so, which was quite good because I’d settled in, I sort of knew what I was doing and if there was a problem I could have spoken to him earlier and said ‘look can you come down’, but there wasn’t so it worked quite well.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: If you did have any problems, would you go to uni first or your supervisor?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: I think I’d go to, I’d definitely go to [manager] and [supervisor] first. Erm, before uni, because I don’t sort of. I think it’s easier just to go and sort it out and they’re very approachable both of them. So things like that I don’t see as a major problem, erm going to them and moaning to them. And I have done. Erm the one time I was having really problems with a couple of people from site not doing what they were meant to be doing and I was getting a bit of a backlash and I actually went and said, ‘look these people have really pissed me off, help, what do I do?’ And she goes, ‘oh, don’t worry, I’ll sort it.’ So it’s nice that I actually felt I could go and talk to her and not, just tell her what I was thinking and feeling.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: So was that because people weren’t doing what they were supposed to be doing?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: What they were meant to be doing and they weren’t listening to what I was saying, erm because I was just (inaudible).

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Is that because you were a student?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: A student, but it’s because in the department I’m not considered just as a student. Yes I’m the IT but when it comes to actually getting down and doing the work, I’m counted as a person and sort of, they realise the importance of an IT because there’s a question at the moment whether they’re going to replace me with another student or whether they’re going to get someone else. And they’re like we can’t actually survive without an IT, so they’re like yes ok, maybe you are quite important. And so they realise. And because I do a lot of work for everyone that it’s that sort of base.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: So you’re an important person. Do you think that there are appropriate facilities for women here?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yeah. (laughing) Definitely because you’ve got occupational health and they do regular medicals as well, so, things like that.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: When you go out on site do you have to wear safety clothing?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yes

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Does that come in women’s sizes?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yes. I don’t think, I think it’s either or really, ‘cos I mean, I think its one size fits all really, most stuff. Erm, and we have our own safety stuff that we wear anyway so it’s not really gender specific like a big coat.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: You spoke a bit about this earlier, but can you think of any other occasions where you feel like the fact that you’re a woman has determined reactions you’ve got from people?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Not at all. I mean if anything, I don’t think it’s an advantage or a disadvantage. I think you have just as good a laugh with everyone, the operators even if they do give you, sort of say things, they’re not being mean or harsh in anyway. Erm, it just means you have a laugh with them. Erm, and it actually gets, erm and if you end up having a laugh with them, they’ll be inclined to do a lot more work for you, which is always a good thing. Like ‘oh, you don’t mind doing that for me do you?’ So it’s quite good in that way, but there’s no prejudicial, so. I think its partly, I don’t know if it’s to do with the fact that you’ve got both top, top, top managers from both research and manufacturing are women, so it shows straight away that there’s no prejudices between women and men.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Do you think that you’re career ambitions have changed as a result of doing the placement?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Definitely. I wasn’t going to do environmental at all. It was only the fact that I was so desperate for a position I was like I’ll apply for anything, I’ll do anything in either energy or environmental. ‘Cos I wanted to get an energy related placement, erm and now I’m here and doing the work, environmental work I think I’ll probably end up going into environmental career. I think I want to do something very similar to what I’m doing now, sort of environmental advisor.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Ok, do you think that your experience here will influence the type of company that you apply for jobs at? Like you were saying that because it’s such a big company, there’s certain support structures in place?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: I don’t know. I’m not too sure. I think I probably will end up working for a big company because of the fact that it’s going to be the type of role I can go into. Erm, because obviously to get a reasonable size environmental team you have to have a lot of people round. So I mean we’ve got 900 people in manufacturing, and erm we’ve got six, seven people in the department. So its sort of getting that sort of size company to get that number of people and get places. ‘Cos I don’t know if I could go into a small company where I was the only environmental manager. I think that’d be sort of too much when I first leave anyway. Maybe in the future I could consider going into a smaller place, but I probably won’t be.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Would you work here if you had the opportunity when you graduated?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Erm, I probably would, if, the only thing that sort of puts me back is it’s location. It’s in the middle of nowhere, it takes two hours to get past London, so there is that sort of disadvantage, but I don’t think, the company looks after it’s people.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Has [company] got other locations in the UK?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: I’m just thinking.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: This is the headquarters isn’t it?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yes it’s the European headquarters. Erm, but we’ve got a couple, there’s one which is [name], but they’re trying to sell it at the moment, up in [name]. And then they’ve got a couple of other sites but then they’ve got a couple of sites in Ireland and sites all round Europe as well. So there are different places where I could work.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Would you like to work abroad? Does that appeal to you?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yes I think it does, but I think the language might be a problem (laughing). Erm, but I could work in America or New Zealand or somewhere like that. But I don’t know. It’s a good company to work for.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Do you think that the placement will help you when you start work?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yes.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Even if you don’t come back to work at [company]?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: I think it’ll, one it will help me get a job, having such a big reputable company on your CV, can’t be a negative thing at all. Erm, and also I think it’s also, the knowledge and sort of hands on experience that I’ve got in the different fields, that I wouldn’t normally have got at uni, erm had I just gone straight through, erm, I just would not have got the sort of experience and sort of getting to know the different places where you can send your waste, sort of different companies, getting to know them. Erm, its just a general knowledge.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Do you think it will help just in terms of settling into a new job, having been in a work environment?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yeah. You know how things roughly work. I mean, yeah different organisations have different structures and obviously you’ve got to get used to them but at the end of the day, if you’ve worked in a big company with lots of different management structures, most places aren’t going to be as big, there’s only a few companies which are as big as [company]. So, erm, if you can survive in a place like this, you can survive anywhere, that’s my thinking anyway.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: I’ve just got a couple of questions left. They are questions that I asked you last time to see if your opinion has changed at all. So, can you give me five words to describe the characteristics of your field of engineering?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: So characteristics of the industry? Erm, erm, I think it’s quite a conscientious one, we’re sort of a hidden, quite stealth area of work. So people think of health and safety, but they don’t think of environmental. It’s not sort of a key. It’s a key one, but it’s not. We’re sort of hidden away, erm, it’s not an obvious one to everyone else. So you have to keep on chipping away and seeing how people react. So it’s sort of hidden in that way. It’s, I don’t know. I think it’s quite a softly, softly sort of, you have to talk to people gently and persuade them that it is a good idea to do this, so it’s quite a persuasive area of work.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: So you have to have good negotiation skills?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yes. I try and persuade them to do something and make them think it’s their idea rather than mine. Because it doesn’t work if you try and force things on them. Erm … what did I say last time?

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: The words that you used last time were more general: challenging

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yeah, I think I’d stick with challenging

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Interesting

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: It is interesting to me, but (laughing).

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Complicated

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Erm, yeah, in some ways but not sort of, there are simple ways of doing things, so I don’t think it is as complicated as I thought it was. It is a big network or a web of things but it all sort of narrows down eventually.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: I guess your opinion of this has changed from what you’ve already told me, but you thought it might be quite ‘offish’ towards women previously?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Erm, yeah. I think I’ve definitely changed on that one, because it isn’t at all. Erm, it’s very open.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: So do you think that you were concerned about that before you started?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: I don’t think I was concerned no. ‘Cos I’ve come from a very male dominated, like my college course was all men, I was the only girl, so, that didn’t bother me, but I thought it was going to be more male dominated, but it’s definitely not.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Were you surprised when you came here and saw how many women were in the team?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: I don’t think I sort of consciously thought about it. Erm.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Ok, I think you may have answered this already, but do you think that there are any advantages or disadvantages to being a woman in engineering?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: No not at all.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Do you think that it is concerning that there aren’t more women in engineering?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Erm, I don’t know because, it is quite hard, because even in the pure engineering departments there are quite a few women working. I mean we’ve got utilities and that’s all, the manager of utilities is a woman and there’s different women in all kinds of different engineering roles on site, so I think it’s definitely opened my eyes up to the fact that there are a lot more women than I thought there would be. I thought it would be the odd one here and there, but yeah, it’s not dominated definitely not, but I think there’s definitely more than there are, what sort of my thoughts were. Sorry that’s …

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: No that’s fine. That’s your experience of this company. Do you think that more generally, more women should be encouraged or provided with opportunities to do engineering?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Definitely, because erm, like seeing that there are women out here, I don’t think people, especially in schools, I don’t think they realise that, they think engineering, they think mechanical, they think (mucky looking?) but and thinking ‘oh it’s not a place for women’, but it is. There is the opportunities, and I think sort of the experience here shows that it’s a growing field, a growing area. There are a lot more women coming in, and I think it is concerning that at school age you don’t think, girls don’t think about coming through and doing sort of science and engineering. They make think sort of lab sciences but not engineering engineering.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Do you think that’s [company] attitude as well, because you said you’ve been doing this Jamboree thing, so they are obviously interested in getting younger people interested.

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yeah, I think they’re just trying to get people interested in science in general. And yeah there was, one of the engineering departments actually had a stand, so they were showing everyone, they weren’t just showing all the boys. So I think [company] are trying to, in some ways, get through. Erm.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Did you get a good response from the kids doing that then?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yeah. We had, they really enjoyed it. And we all did, our stand was all about waste and what to do with the waste and where it goes and stuff like that. Every kid was pretty much getting into it and finding it fun and interesting in, so. I don’t think [company] conscientiously think ‘oh we’ve got to concentrate on all women and all girls. It’s just a sort of general get at everyone in science and engineering. But it needs to be growing really, there needs to be more of a push I think.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
